slides.title: Words as vectors
slides.body:
An **embedding** is a list of numbers — a vector — that represents a word. Instead of treating tokens as arbitrary integers (token 12 has nothing to do with token 13), we place each one at a specific point in a high-dimensional space.

The magic property: **words with similar meanings end up near each other**.

Think of a giant room where every word in English has a location. `dog` and `cat` are near each other because they're both pets. `king` and `queen` are near each other because they're both royalty. `Paris` and `France` are near each other because of geography. This room is the embedding space; each word's location is its embedding vector.

A typical transformer embedding has 768 to 4,096 dimensions — far more than 3, but the geometric intuition still holds.

slides.title: Similarity is direction, not magnitude
slides.body:
When we ask *"how similar are these two words?"*, we usually mean **cosine similarity** — the angle between their embedding vectors. Two vectors pointing in the same direction are maximally similar (cosine = 1); perpendicular vectors are unrelated (cosine = 0); opposite vectors are anti-related (cosine = -1).

Magnitude is mostly ignored in semantic-similarity contexts. A common embedding has length ~1 anyway, after L2 normalization.

Why does this work? Because the model is trained on the **distributional hypothesis**: words that appear in similar contexts get pushed toward similar directions. `king` and `queen` co-occur with similar surrounding words (royal, throne, crown), so the training objective drives their vectors close together.

question.question: Which pair of words would you expect to have the *highest* cosine similarity in a well-trained embedding space?
question.explanation: doctor and nurse co-occur in many similar contexts (hospitals, medicine, patients), so their embeddings are pulled toward similar directions during training. The other pairs share little contextual structure.

slides.title: Where embeddings come from
slides.body:
Embeddings aren't designed by hand — they're **learned**, alongside the rest of the model.

In a transformer, the embedding layer is just a giant matrix `E` of shape `[vocab_size, d_model]`. Token id 42 fetches row 42 of this matrix as its starting vector. During training, gradients flow back into `E` and adjust those rows so that the model's predictions get better.

For a model trained on next-token prediction over hundreds of billions of tokens, the embeddings end up encoding remarkably structured semantic knowledge. The famous `king − man + woman ≈ queen` pattern (Mikolov et al. 2013) emerges from this kind of training.

Modern transformers also **tie** the input embedding matrix to the output projection — the same matrix that turned tokens into vectors at the start is used (transposed) to turn vectors back into token probabilities at the end.

slides.title: How attention uses embeddings
slides.body:
Embeddings aren't the destination — they're the **starting point**. Every transformer layer reads the embedding of each token, computes a new representation that mixes information across tokens via [attention](/wiki/attention), and writes the result back.

The key insight to carry forward: attention computes **dot products between embedding-derived vectors** (queries and keys). High dot product means "these two tokens are aligned in the relevant subspace," which is exactly the geometric relationship we just discussed.

So every concept on this path — positional encoding, attention, multi-head, the transformer block — is operating on this vector geometry. The embedding space is the substrate of meaning that the rest of the network manipulates.
